title: AWS Capacity Largely Sold Out Through 2027, With On Demand Headroom Reserved
gist: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said AWS committed capacity is gone for 2026, largely sold out through 2027 with a good chunk of 2028 allocated, and that AWS could invest well beyond its roughly $220B 2026 capex without it being a poor use of capital. Analyst David Linthicum pushed back that this applies to giant pre-reserved blocks, while practitioners report real shortages even for ordinary on-demand EC2 and across all three major clouds.

insights.claim: Andy Jassy said AWS committed cloud capacity for 2026 is already gone, 2027 is largely sold out and a good chunk of 2028 is sold out, while AWS keeps headroom for On Demand EC2 and Bedrock inference.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Multi-year sold-out compute supports AWS revenue visibility and continued hyperscaler capex for chips, power and data centers.
insights.quote: 2027 is largely sold out. We always leave a certain amount for on demand and our inference service bedrock, or EC2, but largely sold out all the big chunks. A good chunk of 2028 is sold out.

insights.claim: Jassy said Amazon could invest well beyond its roughly $220 billion planned 2026 capital expenditure without it being a poor use of capital; commenters note the $220B is total capex, not AI-only.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Signals upside risk to Amazon capex guidance, bullish for AI-infra suppliers (GPUs, Trainium supply chain, power, construction).

insights.claim: AWS raised Capacity Blocks for ML prices by about 15% uniformly across every region in January, covering P5en, P5e, P5, P4d GPU instances and Trn2/Trn1.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: GPU rental pricing power is holding/rising at hyperscalers, contrary to GPU-glut narratives.
insights.locator: Jassy made the remarks in a video podcast

insights.claim: Amazon's remaining performance obligations disclosure in its third-quarter results will show how much of the committed AWS capacity is contracted revenue.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: RPO/backlog is the metric to check to validate the sold-out claim.

insights.claim: Cloud analyst David Linthicum argues reports overstated AWS's position: Jassy described massive pre-reserved multi-year capacity blocks, not day-to-day enterprise GPU allocation, which he believes is still possible in the console.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Distinguish hyperscale reserved blocks (bought by model labs) from general availability when reading capacity headlines.
insights.quote: that’s not exactly the same thing as "AWS is sold out."

insights.claim: Practitioners report constraints even on ordinary on-demand EC2 instances in recent weeks, with production Kubernetes clusters sometimes concerningly constrained, and one commenter reports insufficient compute from all three major clouds, not limited to GPUs.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Scarcity spreading from GPUs to general compute would broaden pricing power and capex beyond AI accelerators.
insights.quote: Forget spot instances we have trouble getting enough on demand.

insights.claim: Microsoft has released only limited information about Azure East US capacity constraints, and at least one operations team adopted reserved instances to secure capacity against projected growth.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Capacity tightness is cross-hyperscaler, supporting the sector-wide capex cycle.

insights.claim: Capacity scarcity is pushing customers to reserve cloud resources they fear they might need, which Ian Rae calls an anti-cloud pattern that could inflate reservations beyond real demand.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Hoarding-driven reservations can overstate true demand; watch reservation-utilization ratios (EC2 Capacity Manager) for signs of a double-ordering cycle.
insights.quote: folks reserve cloud resources they are worried they might need, which is an anti-cloud pattern
